client: Lately, I’ve been lying awake at night with this tightness in my chest, just staring at my thesis outline but not writing anything. I know the deadline’s getting closer, but between my shifts at the coffee shop and friends expecting me to show up to things, I keep freezing up. Part of me wonders if talking about it will just make me more aware of how behind I am.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of pressure and exhaustion, with your responsibilities pulling you in different directions. The way your voice tightens suggests this isn't just stress about deadlines—it feels more like a deep overwhelm that's making it hard to even start. Would it help to explore how realistic those expectations on yourself truly are?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess my expectations might be unrealistic, but I don't know how to lower them. If I ask for extensions or cancel plans, I feel like I'm failing at everything - being a good student, friend, and employee all at once. The guilt just makes me procrastinate more.
therapist: I hear that shaky frustration in your voice—it sounds like you're caught between what you think you *should* be doing and what actually feels manageable. The guilt you're describing creates this impossible standard where any adjustment feels like failure, when really it might be the wisest choice. What would it look like to challenge that all-or-nothing thinking—where does the evidence show you've actually dropped all the balls at once?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I haven't completely failed at everything yet. But that's the problem - the dread that it's all about to collapse any day now keeps me paralyzed. Like if I take one break or say no to one social thing, suddenly the whole fragile system will fall apart.
therapist: Your voice sounds both weary and tense—like you're holding your breath waiting for everything to crumble, even while part of you knows it hasn't yet. That dread of collapse feels very real in your words, but I wonder if we could examine whether "fragile system" is a thought or a fact—what evidence tells you it would all fall apart from one break?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I see what you're saying, but the evidence is that last semester when I canceled plans to study, two friends stopped inviting me to things. So one break did make part of my life fall apart. Now I'm terrified it'll happen with work if I call in sick, or with my advisor if I ask for an extension.
therapist: I notice your voice gets faster and higher when you talk about that past experience—it still carries a sting, doesn't it? That one painful outcome seems to have become proof that any boundary will cost you relationships, but I wonder if we could look at whether those friends represented all connections, or just one possibility that left space for others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess those two friends weren't my whole social circle... but it still makes me question who actually cares about me versus just wanting me to show up. And now I'm scared to test it with anyone else - what if more people disappear when I can't be available?
therapist: Your voice sounds both hesitant and vulnerable as you share this—it seems that fear of losing connections runs deep, especially after feeling let down before. While that worry feels very real, I wonder if we could explore whether being available all the time has ever truly shown you who cares most deeply about *you*, not just your presence?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never really thought about it that way... Being available all the time does make me feel like people only notice me when I'm there, not when I'm struggling. But setting boundaries still terrifies me - what if I end up completely alone? It feels safer to keep saying yes, even if it’s draining me.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and anxious as you share this—like the fear of ending up alone feels very immediate and overwhelming. That exhaustion from always saying yes seems to be weighing heavily on you, even as the alternative feels terrifying. Would it help to explore what "completely alone" really means—whether it's an absolute truth or perhaps your mind's way of protecting you from past hurts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess "completely alone" feels like being invisible—like if I’m not there, no one will notice or care. It’s hard to imagine that anyone would stick around if I’m not constantly available. But you’re right, it’s exhausting to keep up this act. I just don’t know how to trust that people will still want me around if I’m not always saying yes.
therapist: Your voice speeds up as you talk about feeling invisible—it sounds like this fear taps into something raw about whether you matter just as *you*, not just for what you provide to others. That exhaustion in your tone tells me this "act" is wearing you down, even as the alternative feels risky. What would it look like to test that belief gently—maybe by noticing who checks in when *you're* the one needing support?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That sounds terrifying, honestly. What if I reach out and nobody responds? I've built my whole routine around being the reliable one—if I stop that and people don't check in, it'll confirm my worst fear that I don't matter. But... I'm so tired of pretending I'm fine all the time.
therapist: I hear the exhaustion and vulnerability in your voice—it sounds like this fear of not mattering feels so deeply tied to being "the reliable one" that stepping away from that role feels like risking your whole sense of self. That tiredness you describe suggests this mask of being fine all the time has become too heavy to carry, even as the alternative feels terrifying. What if we approached this not as an all-or-nothing shift, but as small steps to test whether your worth is truly tied to always being available?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Small steps sound less overwhelming, but I'm still scared of the outcome. What if I try something small, like saying no to one plan, and it turns out nobody really cared if I was there? That would just confirm that I’ve been fooling myself all this time. It’s easier to keep pretending than to face that possibility.
therapist: Your voice sounds both shaky and intense as you share this—it’s clear that the fear of confirming your worst fears feels almost unbearable. That hesitation makes sense when stepping back feels like risking everything you’ve built your identity around. But I wonder if we could explore whether caring about you and caring about your presence are truly the same thing—what evidence tells you they’ve always been tied together?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very loud, very rapid speech

client: I see what you're saying, but it’s hard to separate the two when most of my interactions are based on me showing up—whether it’s at work, with friends, or even with my advisor. The idea that people might care about *me* outside of that feels... abstract. It’s not something I’ve ever really experienced, so it’s hard to believe it’s possible.
therapist: Your voice sounds both quiet and strained—it seems this isn’t just skepticism, but a deep, weary resignation that relationships have always been transactional for you. That flatness in your tone tells me how exhausting it must be to feel like your worth is tied to performance, even while part of you longs for something more. What would it look like to explore whether "showing up" is the only glue holding these connections together—or if there might be small moments where care showed up differently?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech
